prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation by chemically induced proximity, from bifunctional PROTACs to molecular glue degraders

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is a genuinely new drug modality that is simple to state: a small molecule brings a ubiquitin ligase to a target and the cell destroys it. It is a game-changer by my own standard, because it has already produced real consequences, with many degraders in clinical trials and a mechanistic explanation of thalidomide and its analogues through cereblon. It is supported by six of eight openings, more broadly than anything else on the shortlist, and the chemistry (ternary-complex design, ligand optimisation, ligase recruitment) is explicit and reproducible across many independent laboratories. Crews and Deshaies conceived and demonstrated the PROTAC concept, and Handa's identification of cereblon anchors the molecular glue branch, so the configuration covers both halves of the field with the three-person limit respected.
statement.case_against: Credit is spread over eight credited names, and any three-person choice leaves out serious contributors: Ciulli (VHL ligands and structural basis of ternary complexes), Gray, Sakamoto, Ito and Kim. No PROTAC has yet been approved as far as I know, so clinical vindication is incomplete, and the field is still moving quickly. The PROTAC and cereblon glue strands arguably have different intellectual origins, so a single citation risks being either vague or unfair to one side. My own first-ranked candidate, Car and Parrinello (B020), has a cleaner attribution story and a longer track record, but it received no support from colleagues, and computational chemistry has been honoured recently (2013 and 2024), which weakens its claim on timing.

responses.point: Aili ranks B044 first and proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa, arguing that induced proximity redefined what a small molecule can do and that the PROTAC and cereblon molecular-glue discoveries are the core of the prize.
responses.response: I agree on the science and, after reading the openings, I move to your trio. In my opening I preferred Ciulli over Handa, but Handa's cereblon work is what explains the thalidomide mechanism, and molecular glues are the most clinically validated branch today. I do share your reservation that dropping Ciulli is a real cost, since his VHL ligands made PROTACs drug-like and gave the structural basis for ternary complexes. I would not call that an error in the configuration, but the citation should be written so that it does not claim Handa's work as PROTAC chemistry.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first but credits David R. Liu alone, emphasising explicit deaminase chemistry, clinical translation and a conventional principal-investigator attribution, while ranking B044 second.
responses.response: I take the chemistry argument seriously and ranked B019 sixth. Where I differ is that sole credit to Liu sits uneasily with the fact that Komor and Gaudelli did the decisive experiments on the cytosine and adenine editors, and Kondo and Nishida's parallel deaminase work muddies priority. The 2020 CRISPR prize also leaves base editing looking like a tool built on a prize already awarded. Degradation does not carry that overlap, which is why I would put it ahead, though I accept that your ranking of B044 second shows we are close.

responses.point: Sparr ranks phase separation first, arguing that biomolecular condensates reframed cell organisation as a physical-chemistry problem with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the core attribution.
responses.response: I ranked B039 last of my eight, so I should explain why. The concept is important and the attribution of Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen is neat, but I am not convinced yet that it is chemistry in the sense of a quantitative, settled mechanism. You yourself note the debate over which in-cell condensates are true equilibrium phases. I would like to see that settle, and ideally see quantitative experimental tests of the physical picture, before I would support it over degraders, which already have clinical consequences.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, ranks nanopore sequencing first for its clean physical principle, mature commercial use and timeliness, and ranks halide perovskites second and B044 fifth.
responses.response: I see the attraction of nanopores as an original physical idea that has already reached users, and the Branton, Deamer and Akeson attribution is workable. My concern is the priority tangle with Kasianowicz and Bayley, which the three-person cap forces us to resolve. I would rate B068 as a serious candidate, but I do not agree that it should rank above degraders, which have wider chemical and therapeutic reach. On perovskites, the stability and toxicity problems you mention are exactly why I am hesitant to call that field settled.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should credit Ciulli instead of or alongside Handa, and whether a one-sentence citation can fairly cover both PROTACs and molecular glues.
Whether the absence of an approved PROTAC drug makes recognition premature compared with candidates with established clinical use such as lipid nanoparticles.
Whether Car and Parrinello (B020) deserve to be advanced despite no support from colleagues in the openings, given recent computational prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B044 from my profile. My only relevant connection is my postdoc collaboration with Arieh Warshel (empirical valence bond), and Warshel is not credited in any shortlisted ballot. As a computational chemist I should be careful about advocating B020, where I have no personal tie to Car or Parrinello but a clear field affinity.
